title: A tiny server that watches its own traffic

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: What if you could see who visits your personal website, which countries they come from, and pay about ten cents a day for the privilege?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Ten cents? Most dashboards charge more than that for a login screen.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That was Antoine's goal. He already ran Caddy at home for Home Assistant, so he built an AWS version: a tiny t4g nano EC2 instance acting as a reverse proxy, with automatic HTTPS, and a small chain of cloud services watching the logs.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Quick refresher. A reverse proxy is the front door that forwards visitors to the real site?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly, like a receptionist. Visitors talk to Caddy, and Caddy hands them to the right place. His first version, around 2021, was a small VPS linked to a server at home through a WireGuard tunnel. The EC2 setup grew from that.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And where do the logs come in?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Caddy writes every request as a JSON line, one file per site, rotated at ten megabytes with five files kept for seven days. Every night, a short Python script using boto3 reads those files and ships them to a CloudWatch log group called reverse proxy.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So CloudWatch becomes the filing cabinet.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right, and then the interesting part starts. A Step Functions workflow runs two Lambda functions in order. The first one, QueryLogsInsights, asks CloudWatch Logs Insights for the visitor addresses from the last twenty-four hours.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: GetGeolocation. It takes that list of addresses, looks each one up on ipinfo dot io, and writes city, region, country, coordinates and organization into a separate geoip log group.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So an address turns into a place on a map.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. A CloudWatch dashboard then puts it all side by side: traffic, error rates, instance CPU and network, and the geolocation results. And since everything is pay-per-run, the whole thing stays cheap, which suits personal-scale traffic.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It did. Today Antoine runs Caddy in Docker on a VPS, provisioned with Terraform and configured with Ansible, and he kept the same per-site JSON logging recipe. The takeaway: with a little Python glue and a few managed services, you get real visibility into your own traffic without a big monitoring bill. The full write-up has the diagrams and the code.
